historical_timeline.summary: Born in Erode; grew up in Kumbakonam.
First of two episodes of dysentery in India (dates approximate).
Operation after a serious illness; married Janaki; second episode of dysentery about this time.
Arrived in England and moved into rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge.
Admitted to a nursing hostel in Cambridge; treated in sanatoria and nursing homes until early 1919.
Reported suicide attempt in the London Underground; the account rests on later recollection.
Elected a Fellow of the Royal Society.
D. A. B. Young proposed hepatic amoebiasis as the cause of his illness.

claims.statement: Srinivasa Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 in his grandmother's house in Erode, in what is now Tamil Nadu, and grew up in Kumbakonam. His father, Kuppuswamy Srinivasa, was a clerk in a cloth merchant's shop, and his mother, Komalatammal, sang devotional songs; the family was Brahmin and poor.

claims.statement: He had no family name in the Western sense. In Tamil usage the father's given name comes first as an initial or prefix, so "Srinivasa" is his father's name and "Ramanujan" is his own given name, the name by which he was known and addressed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the coded name: Ramanujan is the given name; Srinivasa, the patronymic, takes the family-name position.

claims.statement: He had smallpox in December 1889, fell ill after about three months at a college in Madras in 1906, and had a serious illness in 1908 followed by an operation in 1909 and a long recovery.
He had two episodes of dysentery in India, about eleven and eight years before his illness in England.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the modern history of dysentery years ago, the clue that points to amebiasis.

claims.statement: He married Janaki in July 1909, worked as a clerk at the Madras Port Trust from March 1912, wrote to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge in January 1913, sailed for England in March 1914, and moved into rooms at Trinity College, Cambridge, at the end of April 1914.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his modern life as a mathematician far from his wife and family.

claims.statement: An orthodox Brahmin, he was a strict vegetarian. He had trouble with his diet from the start in England; the war that began a few months after his arrival made the foods he needed harder to get, and he cooked for himself, sometimes only once a day or every other day.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the vegetarian diet, the nutritional assessment and the culturally respectful dietary plan.

He fell seriously ill in 1917: from May 1917 he was in a nursing hostel in Cambridge, then a sanatorium in the Mendip Hills in October 1917, Matlock House in Derbyshire from November 1917 to June 1918, Fitzroy House in London from June to December 1918, and Colinette House in Putney at the end of December 1918.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: The evaluation of fever, weight loss and right upper quadrant pain in a 29-year-old mathematician from Tamil Nadu, a strict vegetarian, who came to a research fellowship far from home. The episode works through the differential that divided his historical physicians and later historians, tuberculosis or amebiasis, with modern tests: a chest radiograph, induced sputum for smears, NAAT and culture, an interferon-gamma release assay, stool tests and Entamoeba histolytica serology, and an abdominal ultrasound. The single modern diagnosis is an amebic liver abscess, treated by CDC guidance with metronidazole and then the luminal agent paromomycin; the positive IGRA with negative cultures is latent tuberculosis infection, treated after the abscess with four months of rifampin under the 1911 NTCA/CDC guideline, with the ATS/CDC/IDSA guidelines for diagnosis and treatment. The episode adds a nutrition assessment with vitamin B12 and vitamin D repletion suited to a lacto-vegetarian, a dietary plan built on his own food and rules, PHQ-9 and GAD-7 screening with a structured safety assessment, counseling, and practical support for a student far from home. The modern diagnosis is synthetic and does not settle the historical question.

visit_schedule.purpose: New patient with four weeks of evening fevers and night sweats, weight loss and right upper quadrant pain, in a 29-year-old mathematician from Tamil Nadu who came to a research fellowship here three years ago

Six weeks: recovery, final sputum cultures, liver tests before rifampin, vitamin B12, mood, influenza vaccine
Same-day sick visit for a cold with fever, and the question of an abscess relapse
Periodic adult preventive visit with pre-travel advice
Three months: abscess treatment complete, rifampin month two, blood count, liver tests, vitamins, mood, and plans to visit home

hpi.narrative: Mr. Ramanujan returns two days after his first visit. He had the abdominal ultrasound yesterday morning and gave the second and third induced sputum samples yesterday and this morning, staying in his room in between as asked. He still has evening fevers, last night to 38.4 °C, with sweats, and the dull ache under his right ribs, worse when he breathes in deeply. He is eating little and taking acetaminophen. He has had no diarrhea for several years. He has read about tuberculosis and is frightened of it. He met Dr. Raghunathan of infectious diseases here today.

Entamoeba histolytica antibody positive; stool antigen and microscopy negative, which is common with a liver abscess; two blood cultures without growth after 48 hours. With fever, a tender liver, a single right-lobe abscess, positive serology and dysentery years ago in India, this is an amebic liver abscess rather than a pyogenic one. Dr. Raghunathan agrees. It is not large or in the left lobe and shows no sign of imminent rupture, so it does not need draining now
plan: Metronidazole 750 mg three times a day with food for 10 days; no alcohol (he does not drink)
Then paromomycin 500 mg three times a day for 7 days, not at the same time as metronidazole
Nurse phone check on the third day for the fever; aspiration only if fever persists after 72 hours

Three induced sputum smears and the NAAT on the first sample are negative. Active pulmonary tuberculosis is very unlikely, and his illness is explained by the abscess; he has tuberculosis infection without evidence of disease. Airborne precautions ended. Cultures will be final in six to eight weeks; latent infection is treated only after they are negative and the abscess is treated

He had dysentery twice in India, about eleven and eight years ago, with no record of treatment. Smallpox in childhood and an operation after a serious illness years ago. assessment.assessment: A young man from an endemic area with fever, a tender liver and a single right-lobe abscess, positive Entamoeba histolytica serology and dysentery years ago: an amebic liver abscess. A pyogenic abscess is unlikely with negative blood cultures and no biliary or abdominal source. A negative stool antigen is common with liver abscess and does not argue against the diagnosis. Serology can stay positive for years after an old infection, but in this setting it supports the diagnosis. The abscess is under 10 cm, in the right lobe, without signs of imminent rupture, so medicine alone is the right treatment; aspiration is not needed now

The IGRA shows tuberculosis infection, common in people who grew up in South India. Active pulmonary tuberculosis is very unlikely: the radiograph shows only the changes of the abscess at the right base, and three smears and the NAAT are negative. His illness is explained by the abscess. Metronidazole and paromomycin have no activity against tuberculosis, so treating the abscess will not hide it. Cultures must be final before latent infection is diagnosed and treated

recommendations: Metronidazole 750 mg three times a day with food for 10 days; expect a metallic taste and nausea; stop and call for numbness or tingling
Then paromomycin 500 mg three times a day for 7 days to clear intestinal cysts, started after metronidazole and not at the same time, so that its diarrhea does not confuse the response
Aspiration only if fever persists after 72 hours of metronidazole, the abscess enlarges, or it is in a position to rupture; a phone check on the third day
No repeat imaging if he recovers clinically; abscess cavities can take months to resolve on ultrasound
End airborne precautions now; await the mycobacterial cultures at six to eight weeks

When the cultures are negative and the liver tests are normal, treat latent tuberculosis infection with rifampin 600 mg daily for 4 months, with monthly clinical checks and liver tests at baseline and two months

No tuberculosis notification is needed, since active disease has not been found; report amebiasis to the health department where the jurisdiction requires it. No contact screening is needed for amebiasis acquired years ago
Treat the vitamin B12 and vitamin D deficiency, as Dr. Ashworth plans
